title: Euboean Cumae
greek: et tandem Euboicis Cumarum adlabitur oris
short: Cumae, on the coast west of Naples, was the oldest Greek colony on the Italian mainland, founded from Chalcis in Euboea; hence 'Euboean'.
body: Cumae (Greek Kyme) was founded in the eighth century BC by settlers from Chalcis on the island of Euboea; Conington cites Livy (8.22) for the Chalcidian origin, and Servius explains the epithet in the same way, offering two derivations of the name, from Greek kymata, 'waves', or from the omen of a pregnant woman (enkyos). Conington notes that the colony is later than Aeneas' time: Virgil, as usual, thinks of his own age. The site, a volcanic hill in the Phlegraean Fields near Lake Avernus, held a temple of Apollo and the cave associated with the Sibyl, and the 'Chalcidian height' where Daedalus landed (Chalcidica arce, 6.17) repeats the link. Page describes how the ships are moored with their prows turned seaward and anchored, ready for departure, while Conington explains this as the heroic custom of landing stern first. Servius reports that in some old copies Book VI began here, because Tucca and Varius had moved the two preceding lines to the end of Book V.

title: The Sibyl of Cumae (Deiphobe)
greek: horrendaeque procul secreta Sibyllae, antrum immane; Phoebi Triviaeque sacerdos, Deiphobe Glauci
short: The Sibyl of Cumae, priestess of Apollo and Trivia, here named Deiphobe daughter of Glaucus, is Aeneas' guide through the underworld.
body: Sibyls were inspired prophetesses at various sites; the Cumaean Sibyl mattered most to Rome, since the Sibylline Books, a collection of oracles in her name, were kept by the state and consulted in crises. Page tells the story of their purchase by Tarquin and notes that Augustus moved them to his new temple of Apollo on the Palatine (dedicated 28 BC), to which Aeneas' vow of a marble temple and the safe-keeping of her oracles (6.69-74) alludes. Conington accepts Henry's view that the Sibyl's cave is the inner sanctuary of Apollo's temple, and Page describes the arrangement: sacred grove, temple doors, and behind them the cave cut in the rock with a hundred mouths. Virgil names her Deiphobe, daughter of Glaucus, and makes her priestess of Phoebus and Trivia, Apollo and Hecate-Diana. She was famously long-lived (longaeva, 6.321): in Ovid, Apollo granted her as many years as grains of sand she could hold (Metamorphoses 14.130-53). Helenus had foretold this meeting in Book III (3.441-60).

title: The doors of Daedalus; Icarus
greek: Daedalus, ut fama est, fugiens Minoia regna... bis conatus erat casus effingere in auro, bis patriae cecidere manus
short: The temple doors carved by Daedalus tell his Cretan story: Androgeos, the Athenian tribute, Pasiphae and the Minotaur, the Labyrinth. Icarus' fall he could not carve.
body: Daedalus, the Athenian craftsman, escaped from Minos' Crete on wings and was said to have landed at Cumae, where he dedicated the wings to Apollo and built the temple. One door shows the death of Androgeos, son of Minos, and the penalty imposed on Athens: seven sons a year, chosen by lot, sent to the Minotaur (the 'children of Cecrops' are Athenians). The other shows Crete: Pasiphae's monstrous passion for the bull, the Minotaur, and the Labyrinth, which Daedalus himself unravelled for Ariadne with a thread. The apostrophe to Icarus is the emotional climax: twice the father tried to shape his son's fall in gold, 'twice the father's hands fell' (6.32-3). Conington supports the view that the doors belong to the temple whose inner shrine is the cave, and summarises the scene; Page notes that the Sibyl's arrival interrupts Aeneas' gazing. Like the pictures of Troy at Carthage (1.453-93), the doors invite him to read a story that mirrors his own: a maze, a father's grief for a son, an unfinished work.

title: The Sibyl possessed: 'deus, ecce deus'
greek: deus, ecce deus!
short: At the threshold the Sibyl is seized by Apollo: her face, colour and hair change and her voice becomes more than mortal.
body: Servius explains the cry as the words of one possessed: she shows the god, who is visible to her alone, because the nearness of the temple has already breathed his power upon her (adflata numine). He also warns readers to note exactly when she is full of the god and when she has set him aside, since her later words about Misenus are spoken without inspiration. Page compares Aeschylus' Agamemnon, where the chorus calls Cassandra 'god-borne' (Ag. 1150) and where she is possessed in the same way, and explains the image Virgil develops at 6.77-102: the priestess struggles like an untamed horse to shake the god from her breast, while Apollo 'clashes the reins and plies the goad'. Conington notes the same metaphor in Phoebi patiens, 'submitting to Phoebus', used as of a horse that endures the whip. The violence of the god's mastery over his virgin priestess has a sexual undertone that many readers have noticed. The oracle she then utters (6.83-97) is the programme of Books VII-XII.

title: 'Another Achilles' (alius Akhilleus): the Sibyl's oracle
greek: alius Latio iam partus Achilles, natus et ipse dea
short: The Sibyl foretells a second Trojan War in Latium, with Turnus as 'another Achilles', also the son of a goddess.
body: Servius identifies the new Akhilleus as Turnus and compares Eclogue 4.34-5 ('there will be another Tiphys, another Argo'), the idea that history repeats itself; Page notes that Turnus' mother is the nymph Venilia, and explains addita Iuno as Juno 'fastened on' the Trojans, never to be shaken off. Every element of the Iliad is promised again: a Simois, a Xanthus, a Greek camp, a hostile Juno, and 'again an alien bride the cause of all that Teucrian woe' (6.93-4), Lavinia in the role of Helen, though this time it is the Trojan who comes for another man's promised bride. Servius comments that the Sibyl 'wraps truth in obscurity' (obscuris vera involvens, 6.100), as Apollo is called Loxias, 'the oblique'. The help that will come 'from a Greek city' (6.97) is, as Servius explains, Pallanteum, the town of the Arcadian Evander on the future site of Rome (Book VIII). The roles of the Iliad are reversed: the Trojans are now the invaders, and the goddess-born champion is their enemy.

anchor: easy is the descent into hell
title: 'Easy is the descent to Avernus' (facilis descensus Averno)
greek: facilis descensus Averno... sed revocare gradum superasque evadere ad auras, hoc opus, hic labor est
short: The most quoted lines of Book VI: the way down to the dead is easy; the return to the upper air is the real task.
body: Averno is a dative of motion ('to Avernus'), as Page explains. Avernus was the crater lake near Cumae believed to be an entrance to the underworld; its name was popularly derived from Greek aornos, 'birdless', because birds were said to die in its fumes (6.239-42). The gate of Dis stands open night and day, since everyone dies; Conington compares the Greek picture of Hades as a host who receives all comers. Only a few, 'whom just Jupiter loved or burning virtue raised to heaven', have returned. Page notes how pauci and potuere are made emphatic, the second answering the potuit of Aeneas' own appeal to the precedents of Orpheus, Pollux, Theseus and Hercules (6.119-23), and how ardens suits virtue that rises to the fiery aether. Hoc opus, hic labor est became proverbial for any hard task. The lines also invited moral allegory: Servius, on the golden bough that follows, reads the descent as a lesson in the right life by which souls return above, with reference to the Pythagorean letter Y.

title: The golden bough
greek: latet arbore opaca aureus et foliis et lento vimine ramus, Iunoni infernae dictus sacer
short: The golden bough, sacred to Proserpine ('nether Juno'), is Aeneas' passport to the underworld; it will yield only to the man whom fate calls.
body: Conington says we cannot tell whether the golden bough is Virgil's invention, though Heyne argued from 6.409 ('the fated rod so long unseen') that it came from an older story; commentators have collected possible inspirations: the suppliant's branch, branches used in purification, the golden wand of Hermes, a gilded bough in the mysteries of Isis, and the golden fleece hanging in a grove. Servius offers both a 'popular' explanation and an allegory. The first links it with the cult of Diana at Aricia, where a runaway slave who broke a bough from a sacred tree could fight the priest for his office, the custom J. G. Frazer made the starting point of The Golden Bough (1890). The second reads it as virtue, with reference to the Pythagorean Y. 'Nether Juno' (Iuno inferna) is Proserpine, queen of the dead, to whom the bough is her due gift (6.142). When found, it is compared to mistletoe, which stays green on a 'foreign tree' in midwinter (6.205-9), and it is fixed at the threshold of Elysium as an offering (6.636).

title: The 'hesitating' bough (cunctantem)
greek: corripit Aeneas extemplo avidusque refringit cunctantem
short: The Sibyl said the bough would come 'willingly and easily' to the man fate called; yet Aeneas breaks it off 'hesitating' (cunctantem). The word has been argued over since antiquity.
body: The Sibyl's condition was explicit: the bough will follow 'willing and easy' if the fates call you, and otherwise no force will break it (6.146-8). Aeneas seizes it 'at once' and 'eagerly' (avidus) breaks it off, 'lingering' (cunctantem). Servius saw the problem and offered three answers: the word is relative to avidus, since to a man so eager no speed would be fast enough, 'for we cannot call slow what followed by fate'; or it refers to the nature of gold, soft and pliant; or it means 'heavy'. Modern critics have divided further. David West compared the bough to Excalibur, a talisman that yields to the chosen hero; R. A. Brooks (1953) reads the episode as showing Aeneas' ignorance of the full implications of his destiny, and Charles Segal sees in the bough's momentary resistance an anticipation of the loss of innocence; and R. F. Thomas has argued that Servius' efforts to explain it away show that such readings were already current in antiquity. The same word describes Dido lingering in her chamber before the hunt (4.133), and Turnus in his final moment (cunctanti, 12.919).

title: Misenus, Hector's trumpeter
greek: Misenum Aeoliden, quo non praestantior alter aere ciere viros Martemque accendere cantu
short: Misenus, once Hector's trumpeter, drowned by a jealous Triton, gives his name to Cape Misenum on the Bay of Naples; his funeral is a picture of Roman rites.
body: Conington explains that a legend of Aeneas' landing included a comrade Misenus who named the headland, Capo Miseno, the station of the Roman fleet in Virgil's day; in one version he was Aeneas' pilot, which may be why Virgil divides that role between him and Palinurus. 'Aeolid' probably means son of a Trojan named Aeolus (killed at 12.542-7) rather than of the wind-god. Page notes the pathetic repetition Misenum... Misenum and the ringing sounds of aere ciere viros Martemque accendere cantu. The ancient Life of Virgil preserves a story about these lines: the poet's freedman Eros recalled that at a recitation Virgil completed two half-lines on the spot, 'quo non praestantior alter' and 'Martemque accendere cantu', and ordered them written in at once. Misenus challenged the gods with his conch and Triton drowned him: a small fable of human presumption. His funeral (6.212-35), with pyre, washing and anointing, purple coverings, the torch held with face averted, bones gathered in a bronze urn and the purification of the mourners, is detailed Roman custom; Page notes that cypress was always associated with death.

anchor: ah keep apart, O ye unsanctified
title: 'Away, away, you uninitiated!' (procul, o procul este, profani)
greek: procul, o procul este, profani
short: The Sibyl's cry is the formula that excluded the uninitiated from sacred rites: the descent is framed as an initiation.
body: Profani are literally those 'in front of the shrine' (pro fano), that is, outside it; Servius glosses the word as 'you who are not initiated', giving the Greek equivalents amyetoi and bebeloi. Conington and Page compare the opening of Callimachus' Hymn to Apollo ('Away, away, whoever is sinful'), and Conington notes that the uninitiated were warned off at the beginning of the mysteries. The cry comes at dawn as the earth groans, the woods move and dogs howl at the coming of the goddess (Servius: Proserpine herself), after the night sacrifice of black victims to Hecate, to Night and Earth, to Proserpine and to the king of the dead. Aeneas' companions must stay behind; Aeneas, sword drawn, follows the Sibyl into the cave. Many readers have compared the whole journey to the Eleusinian mysteries, with their darkness, terrors and final vision of light, and Servius himself says that 'to go down to the underworld' here means 'to celebrate the rites of Proserpine' (on 6.136).

anchor: They went darkling through the dusk
title: 'They went dark beneath the lonely night' (ibant obscuri sola sub nocte)
greek: ibant obscuri sola sub nocte per umbram
short: A celebrated line of exchanged epithets: the travellers are 'dark' and the night 'lonely', where one would expect 'alone' and 'dark night'.
body: The expected order would be 'they went alone (soli) beneath the dark (obscura) night'. Servius names the figure, hypallage (the exchange of epithets), and offers an alternative: 'beneath a night that was only night', with nothing else present. Conington records that a few manuscripts actually read obscura soli, the more ordinary arrangement, and keeps the received text. The exchange makes the travellers part of the darkness and the night itself lonely. The passage is preceded by a solemn invocation of the gods of the dead and of Chaos and Phlegethon (6.264-7), modelled, Conington notes, on Homer's invocation before the Catalogue of Ships; Page stresses the negative vocabulary of a world where the dead are 'silent'. He also admires the heavy spondees of 6.268 and the plain verb ibant, which carries the reader from the upper to the lower world almost unawares, and explains the simile that follows (per incertam lunam sub luce maligna) as a moon that gives no sure sign of its presence, rather than fitful moonlight.

title: The vestibule of Orcus: personified evils and phantom monsters
greek: vestibulum ante ipsum primisque in faucibus Orci... consanguineus Leti Sopor
short: At the entrance of the underworld sit the personified evils of life, from Grief and Disease to War and Discord; then an elm of false Dreams and phantom monsters.
body: Page explains vestibulum and fauces from the plan of a Roman house, where the street door was set back to leave a recess, the vestibule, before the passage into the hall; the underworld is pictured as a great house with life's evils lodged at its entrance. Sleep is 'kinsman of Death', a relationship as old as Homer, where Sleep and Death are twin brothers (Iliad 14.231, 16.671-5), and the pairing prepares for the gates of Sleep at the end of the book. Page takes the 'avenging Cares' as the stings of conscience. In the middle stands an elm under whose leaves cling idle Dreams. The monsters that follow, Centaurs, Scyllas, hundred-handed Briareus, the Hydra of Lerna, the Chimaera, Gorgons, Harpies and the three-bodied Geryon, are mere images: when Aeneas draws his sword, the Sibyl reminds him that they are thin lives without bodies, 'flitting in the hollow semblance of form' (6.290-4). The scene teaches the conditions of the underworld before the journey proper begins.

title: Charon, ferryman of the dead
greek: portitor has horrendus aquas et flumina servat terribili squalore Charon
short: The squalid old ferryman of the dead, who admits only the buried to his boat.
body: Portitor properly meant a collector of harbour dues, then a man who takes a fare for carrying passengers, and so a ferryman; Conington notes that Virgil had already used it of Charon in the Georgics (4.502) and that Charon is later than Homer, who has no ferryman. Pausanias (10.28.2) reports that the early epic Minyas mentioned him and that Polygnotus painted him in his picture of the underworld at Delphi; the coin placed in the mouth of the dead was his fare. Page accordingly takes inops at 6.325 (Mackail's 'helpless') as 'poor', lacking the coin. Virgil's portrait is grim and physical: a mass of white beard, eyes of flame, a filthy cloak knotted at the shoulder, poling his rust-coloured boat (ferruginea cumba), old, but with a god's green old age. When he takes Aeneas aboard, the boat groans and takes in water under the weight of a living man (6.413-14), an effect like the groaning of Diomedes' chariot-axle under the weight of Athena in Iliad 5.838-9.

title: Simile: the dead as falling leaves and migrating birds
greek: quam multa in silvis autumni frigore primo lapsa cadunt folia, aut ad terram gurgite ab alto quam multae glomerantur aves
short: The crowds of the dead are as many as leaves falling at the first frost or birds flocking south: a simile with a long ancestry and a longer afterlife.
body: Homer compared the generations of men to leaves (Iliad 6.146-9), and Bacchylides (5.63-7) compared the ghosts Heracles met in Hades to leaves on the windy slopes of Ida. Conington finds the closest model in Apollonius (4.216-17) and compares Virgil's own simile of birds in Georgics 4.473-4. Page quotes Bowen's translation and remarks how well both images suit ghosts: their number, lightness and helpless drift with the season. The scene ends in one of Virgil's most admired lines: 'they stood pleading for the first passage across, and stretched forth passionate hands to the farther shore' (tendebantque manus ripae ulterioris amore, 6.314). Dante imitates the leaves for the souls at Acheron (Inferno 3.112-17), and Milton, as Page notes, for the fallen angels lying 'thick as autumnal leaves that strow the brooks in Vallombrosa' (Paradise Lost 1.302-3).

title: The unburied dead
greek: haec omnis, quam cernis, inops inhumataque turba est
short: The unburied must wander a hundred years on the bank before Charon will take them across: burial is a religious duty owed to every dead person.
body: Conington notes that the belief that only the buried can join the dead goes back to Homer: the ghost of Patroclus begs Akhilleus for burial because the other ghosts keep him from crossing the river (Iliad 23.71-4), and Elpenor asks Odysseus for a tomb (Odyssey 11.51-80). He adds Heyne's remark that the belief was humane in its effect, encouraging even savage peoples to bury the dead. Page takes inops as 'poor', without the coin for the fare, and sedibus as the grave, man's 'long home'. The hundred years is Virgil's detail. The rule explains the urgency of Misenus' funeral and the scene with Palinurus that follows, and it gives force to Dido's curse that Aeneas should fall 'unburied on a waste of sand' (4.620). Leucaspis and Orontes, lost in the storm of Book I, are the first of these dead whom Aeneas recognises (6.333-6).

title: Palinurus in the underworld
greek: ecce gubernator sese Palinurus agebat, qui Libyco nuper cursu
short: The ghost of the drowned helmsman tells a story that differs from the narrator's in Book V, and is promised a tomb and a headland bearing his name.
body: Palinurus says that no god drowned him: he fell, tearing away the rudder, drifted for three stormy nights, reached Italy, and was killed by the local people as he clung to the rocks. In Book V the god Sleep threw him overboard on a calm sea (5.854-60). Other details differ too: there the voyage was from Sicily, here he speaks of the 'Libyan voyage' (Page: the voyage from Libya). Scholars have explained the differences as signs of an unrevised poem, as Palinurus' ignorance of the god's part, or as a deliberate contrast of perspectives. Conington compares Odysseus' two days in the sea (Odyssey 5.388-9). Page discusses the apparent hysteron proteron 'throw earth on me and seek the harbour of Velia' (6.365-6). The Sibyl refuses to let him cross unburied but promises that the neighbouring peoples, warned by portents, will build his tomb and that the place will keep his name for ever; Capo Palinuro in southern Italy still does.

title: The 'Amphrysian' prophetess (Amphrysia vates)
greek: quae contra breviter fata est Amphrysia vates
short: A learned epithet: the Sibyl is 'Amphrysian' because she serves Apollo, who once kept the herds of King Admetus by the river Amphrysus in Thessaly.
body: Servius tells the story: Apollo, stripped of his divinity by the angry Jupiter for killing the Cyclopes (who had made the thunderbolt that slew his son Asclepius), tended the herds of Admetus by the Thessalian river Amphrysus. Virgil calls Apollo 'the shepherd from the Amphrysus' (pastor ab Amphryso) at the opening of Georgics 3, and the Sibyl, as Apollo's priestess, inherits the epithet. Servius calls it a 'far-fetched epithet' (longe petitum epitheton), and Conington and Page explain it the same way. Such allusive titles, which name a god through an obscure episode of his myth, are typical of the learned Hellenistic manner that Virgil absorbed from Callimachus and the Roman 'new poets'. The speech it introduces is brisk and authoritative: there is 'no such plot here', Cerberus may bark for ever, Proserpine may keep her honour, and the sight of the golden bough silences Charon.

title: The untimely dead: infants, the falsely condemned, suicides
greek: infantumque animae flentes in limine primo... nec vero hae sine sorte datae, sine iudice, sedes
short: Beyond the river lie those who died before their time: infants, those executed on false charges, and suicides, each in their own region, under the judgment of Minos.
body: Page notes the belief that those who died prematurely could not fully enter the world below, citing a line of Plautus, but warns against treating Virgil's arrangement as a theological system: unlike Dante or Milton, he is not teaching a doctrine. Conington suggests that the infants cry 'on the very threshold' with reference to the Roman custom of burying very young infants under the eaves of the house rather than in a cemetery. Those condemned on false charges have their cases heard again: Minos acts like the president (quaesitor) of a Roman criminal court, shaking the urn from which the jury was chosen by lot and examining 'lives and charges' (Page). The suicides now long to endure poverty and hard labour in the upper air, but Styx 'nine times poured between' confines them. The arrangement weighs on what follows, since Dido, a suicide, is placed not here but among those destroyed by love, the next region.

title: The Fields of Mourning (Lugentes Campi)
greek: Lugentes Campi; sic illos nomine dicunt
short: The 'Mourning Fields' hold those whom love destroyed: a gallery of tragic heroines among whom Dido now walks.
body: Page calls the name 'a phrase worthy of Bunyan, and apparently Virgil's own'; Servius offers a fanciful etymology, as if lugentes were lucis egentes, 'lacking light', which he thinks suits lovers. The women are victims of illicit, jealous or fatal love: Phaedra, who loved her stepson Hippolytus; Procris, killed by her husband's spear after a test of jealousy; Eriphyle, who betrayed her husband for a necklace and was killed by her son; Evadne, who threw herself on her husband's pyre; Pasiphae; Laodamia, who died when her husband Protesilaus returned from the dead for a few hours; and Caeneus, born a woman, made a man, and in death restored to her first shape. The list draws on Odysseus' catalogue of heroines in Odyssey 11.225-332, which includes Phaedra, Procris and Eriphyle. They hide in myrtle groves, the plant of Venus, and Page quotes Wagner: the fields are wide because such souls love solitude. Dido's presence among them is significant: she is classed not with the suicides but with those destroyed by love.

title: Aeneas meets Dido: 'invitus, regina'
greek: invitus, regina, tuo de litore cessi
short: Aeneas' plea to Dido's ghost borrows, almost word for word, a line of Catullus spoken by a lock of hair; Dido answers with silence and turns away to Sychaeus.
body: Aeneas sees her dimly 'as one sees or thinks he sees the moon rising through clouds', a simile Page traces to Apollonius 4.1479-80. His oath echoes Catullus 66.39, where the lock of Queen Berenice's hair, cut off and set among the stars, says 'unwillingly, O queen, I left your head' (invita, o regina, tuo de vertice cessi). Whether the echo is meant to undercut Aeneas, by putting a playful line into a moment of tragic weight, or simply borrows a beautiful phrase, is debated. Dido's response is modelled, as Conington notes, on the silence of Ajax in Odyssey 11.543-64, who will not speak to Odysseus because of an old grievance. She stands 'no more moved than hard flint or Marpesian rock': Servius and Conington explain Marpessos as a mountain on Paros, so that she is like Parian marble. Then she flees to Sychaeus, who 'responds to her distresses'. The roles of Book IV are reversed: now Aeneas pleads and weeps, and Dido is unmoved.

title: Deiphobus and Helen's betrayal
greek: Deiphobum vidit, lacerum crudeliter ora
short: Priam's son, Helen's husband after Paris' death, appears mutilated and tells how Helen betrayed him to Menelaus on Troy's last night.
body: After Paris was killed Deiphobus married Helen, and in the sack of Troy Menelaus killed him in his house (the Odyssey alludes to Odysseus and Menelaus going to the house of Deiphobus, 8.517-20). His face, hands, ears and nose are mutilated, the marks of a shameful death. Aeneas had built him an empty tomb (cenotaph) on the Rhoetean shore and called his name three times, the rite for one whose body could not be recovered. Deiphobus' account of Helen, leading a feigned Bacchic dance, signalling to the Greeks with a torch from the citadel, and removing his sword from under his pillow, does not match Book II, where Sinon released the Greeks from the horse (2.254-9). Conington suggests reconciling them (Helen's torch signalled the fleet, Sinon opened the horse) but thinks it simpler to admit a different version. Page explains the details of the speech. Deiphobus' parting words, 'Go, glory of our people, go, enjoy a fairer fate', are the last voice of the Trojan past before the road divides between Tartarus and Elysium.

title: Tartarus and Rhadamanthus
greek: Gnosius haec Rhadamanthus habet durissima regna castigatque auditque dolos subigitque fateri
short: The Sibyl describes Tartarus, the walled prison of the wicked ringed by the fiery river Phlegethon, where the Cretan judge Rhadamanthus extorts confessions and punishes.
body: Rhadamanthus, son of Jupiter and Europa (Servius) and brother of Minos, comes from Cnossos (Gnosius) in Crete. In Homer he dwells in the Elysian plain (Odyssey 4.563-4); in Plato he judges the dead. Here, as Conington notes after Heyne, his office resembles that of the Roman tresviri capitales or the Athenian Eleven rather than a judge's, since the souls are presumed guilty: he 'chastises and hears their guile, and forces them to confess'. Page discusses the famous inversion of punishment before hearing, which others treat as hysteron proteron, and argues that the lash is used to extort confession. Tartarus is a fortress of adamant with an iron tower, guarded by the Fury Tisiphone, and as deep below as heaven is high above. Aeneas does not enter; the Sibyl, taught by Hecate, describes it. Its inmates are mythical rebels against the gods (Titans, the Aloadae, Salmoneus, Tityos, Ixion) and also Roman sinners: those who hated a brother, struck a parent, cheated a client, hoarded wealth, committed adultery or sold their country.

title: Phlegyas' warning (discite iustitiam moniti); Theseus
greek: sedet aeternumque sedebit infelix Theseus, Phlegyasque miserrimus omnes admonet: 'discite iustitiam moniti et non temnere divos'
short: Phlegyas, eternally punished, cries to all the dead: 'Learn justice, being warned, and do not despise the gods.' Beside him Theseus 'sits and shall sit for ever'.
body: Phlegyas, king of the Lapiths and father of Ixion, was said to have burned Apollo's temple at Delphi, which, as Conington observes after Servius, explains the second half of his warning: his crime was sacrilege as well as injustice. Conington shows that Virgil imitates Pindar, Pythian 2.21-4, where Ixion on his winged wheel proclaims to mortals that they must repay their benefactors with kindness, and rejects Henry's view that 'not to slight the gods' merely repeats 'learn justice'. The fate of Theseus raises a different problem. Servius notes that 'he shall sit for ever' goes 'against the common account', in which Hercules freed him, and adds that poets often vary their myths. The same Theseus was named by Aeneas himself among those who had gone down and returned (6.122). The sentence 'discite iustitiam moniti' became a famous moral tag, though it is addressed to an audience of the damned who can no longer profit from it.

title: Elysium: 'the groves of the Blessed'
greek: devenere locos laetos et amoena virecta fortunatorum nemorum sedesque beatas
short: Elysium, the 'groves of the Blessed', has its own sun and stars; its inhabitants exercise, dance and sing, and include heroes, priests, poets and benefactors.
body: Page connects fortunatorum with the Fortunate Isles or Islands of the Blessed, placed in the far west, and compares Homer's Olympus, untroubled by wind or rain, with a cloudless brightness spread over it (Odyssey 6.42-5), as well as the Elysian plain (Odyssey 4.563-8). Virgil's Elysium is a world of light ('they know their own sun and their own stars') given to the pursuits of the good life: athletics, dance, poetry, chariots and horses. Orpheus, 'the Thracian priest' and founder of mysteries, plays the seven-stringed lyre; Servius connects its seven notes with the music of the planetary spheres. Musaeus, whom Servius calls the first theologian after Orpheus, stands tallest in the crowd. Its population is defined by merit: those wounded for their country, chaste priests, poets who spoke worthily of Apollo, inventors who improved life, and those who earned remembrance by service, all wearing the white fillet. Before entering, Aeneas fixes the golden bough at the threshold (6.635-6). The idea of a reward for civic virtue recalls Cicero's Dream of Scipio.

title: The thrice-attempted embrace
greek: ter conatus ibi collo dare bracchia circum; ter frustra comprensa manus effugit imago, par levibus ventis volucrique simillima somno
short: Aeneas tries three times to embrace his father's ghost, which slips away like wind or a dream: the same lines he used of Creusa in Book II.
body: Page and Conington both note that the three lines repeat 2.792-4, where Aeneas tried to embrace the ghost of Creusa. Their model is Odyssey 11.204-8, where Odysseus tries three times to embrace the ghost of his mother Anticleia, and she flies from his hands 'like a shadow or a dream'. The repetition binds Aeneas' two great losses, wife and father, and reminds the reader that the shades have no bodies, as the Sibyl warned when Aeneas drew his sword on the phantoms at the entrance (6.290-4). The comparison to 'winged sleep' (volucri simillima somno) also looks forward to the gates of Sleep at the end of the book. Anchises' greeting just before ('Art thou come at last, and hath thy love conquered the difficult road?', 6.687-8) is one of the tenderest speeches in the poem, and his fear that 'the realm of Libya might work thee harm' (6.694) briefly recalls Dido.

title: Anchises' doctrine of the soul and rebirth
greek: spiritus intus alit, totamque infusa per artus mens agitat molem et magno se corpore miscet
short: Anchises explains that a divine spirit animates the universe; souls are stained by the body, purged after death, and after a thousand years drink of Lethe to be born again.
body: Conington summarises the doctrine: one great spirit pervades nature, the anima mundi that Virgil had mentioned in Georgics 4.219-27 without committing himself to it; in men it is clogged by the body, so that after death a purification is needed, after which the souls are sent back to animate new bodies. Servius' note reads it in terms of the four elements and a divine spirit infused through them, from which body and mind respectively derive. The sources are mixed: the world-spirit is Stoic; the body as prison, the judgment of souls and the thousand-year cycle recall Plato (the myth of Er, Republic 10.614b-621d); purgation by wind, water and fire and the return to new bodies have Pythagorean and Orphic roots. Page notes Virgil's philosophical interests, citing Donatus' report that he planned to devote the rest of his life to philosophy. The doctrine has a narrative function: it explains why the souls crowding by Lethe, compared to bees in a summer meadow (6.707-9), are the future Romans Anchises will now show his son.

title: Augustus Caesar, divi genus
greek: Augustus Caesar, divi genus, aurea condet saecula qui rursus Latio regnata per arva Saturno quondam
short: Augustus, 'son of a god' (the deified Julius Caesar), will found again the golden age of Saturn in Latium and extend Rome's rule beyond the stars.
body: Page explains divi genus: Julius Caesar received divine honours after his death, and Augustus styled himself Divi filius on his coins. Saturn, the old Italian god of sowing, ruled Latium in the golden age, as Evander will tell in Book VIII (8.319-25); Page notes the pointed use of arva, 'ploughlands', for Saturn's realm. The empire will reach the Garamantes of the Sahara and the Indians, and lands 'beyond the paths of the year and the sun' where Atlas turns the sky. Comparisons with Hercules, who crossed the world to take the bronze-footed hind, the Erymanthian boar and the Hydra of Lerna, and with Bacchus (Liber), who drove his tiger-chariot from Nysa, make Augustus a benefactor-conqueror destined for divinity. The placement is striking: he appears out of chronological order, straight after Romulus, so that founder and refounder stand side by side, before the parade returns to the kings. Anchises then asks whether they still hesitate to extend their valour by deeds (6.806-7): the vision is meant to spur Aeneas, and Virgil's readers, to action.

title: Brutus the avenger and the recovered fasces
greek: animamque superbam ultoris Bruti, fascesque videre receptos
short: Lucius Junius Brutus expelled the Tarquins and became the first consul; he had his own sons executed for plotting to restore the kings.
body: Page tells the story: after Sextus Tarquin's rape of Lucretia, Brutus led the rising that expelled Tarquin the Proud (traditionally 510/509 BC), was elected one of the first two consuls, and, when his two sons joined a conspiracy to restore the monarchy, ordered their execution (Livy 2.3-5). The fasces, the bundle of rods and axe carried by the lictors, symbolised the consul's power of punishment; 'recovered' fasces means power restored to the people. Conington points out that Virgil does not give Tarquin his traditional epithet superbus ('proud') but transfers it to Brutus' 'proud soul', apparently on purpose. The comment that follows, 'unhappy man, however later ages shall view the deed' (infelix, utcumque ferent ea facta minores), shows Virgil's ambivalence: love of country and limitless desire for praise will prevail, but the father who kills his sons is pitied. For an Augustan reader the name Brutus also recalled Caesar's assassin, who claimed descent from the first consul.

anchor: father-in-law descending from the Alpine barriers
title: Caesar and Pompey: father-in-law and son-in-law
greek: aggeribus socer Alpinis atque arce Monoeci descendens, gener adversis instructus Eois
short: Two souls in matching armour are Julius Caesar and Pompey, father-in-law and son-in-law, whose civil war Anchises begs them to renounce before they are born.
body: Page explains: Pompey married Caesar's daughter Julia, who died in 54 BC, and Caesar defeated him at Pharsalus in 48 BC. Caesar comes down from the Alps and 'the citadel of Monoecus'; Servius explains that this was the harbour of Hercules Monoecus in Liguria (modern Monaco), the name meaning 'dwelling alone', either because Hercules lived there alone or because no other god shared his temple. Pompey faces him with the armies of the East. Their 'equal arms' mark a civil war of Roman against Roman (Page compares Lucan's 'standards against standards, eagles matched with eagles'); Conington adds that the phrase also suggests their natural concord and equal generalship. Anchises' appeal, 'and thou, be thou first to forgive, who drawest thy descent from heaven', is addressed to Caesar, descendant of Venus. It is a remarkable moment in a pageant of glory: the founder of Augustus' family is asked to lay down his weapons, and Rome's civil wars are presented as the nation turning its strength against its own heart.

title: Fabius Cunctator: 'unus qui nobis cunctando restituis rem'
greek: tu Maximus ille es, unus qui nobis cunctando restituis rem
short: Quintus Fabius Maximus 'Cunctator', the Delayer, saved Rome from Hannibal by refusing battle; Virgil adapts the famous line of Ennius about him.
body: Fabius, dictator in 217 BC after the disaster at Lake Trasimene, wore Hannibal down by shadowing his army and refusing pitched battle, which earned him the name Cunctator. Page and Conington note that the line is taken almost verbatim from Ennius' Annals, 'unus homo nobis cunctando restituit rem' ('one man by delaying restored the state for us'), preserved by Cicero (De officiis 1.84) and others; Virgil turns it into the second person, so that Anchises addresses Fabius directly. The quotation honours Ennius, Rome's first national epic poet, at the climax of the catalogue. The Fabii were a great clan, and 'whither do you hurry me, weary, O Fabii?' suggests the crowd of their heroes. The verb cunctor links Fabius, for whom delay was salvation, with the bough that 'lingers' (cunctantem, 6.211) and Dido 'lingering' in her chamber (4.133), a connection readers may weigh for themselves.

title: The Roman arts: 'tu regere imperio populos, Romane, memento'
greek: excudent alii spirantia mollius aera... tu regere imperio populos, Romane, memento (hae tibi erunt artes), pacisque imponere morem, parcere subiectis et debellare superbos
short: Others, the Greeks, will excel in sculpture, oratory and astronomy; Rome's art is government: to impose peace, spare the conquered and war down the proud.
body: Page calls these lines the noblest expression of Roman ambition and their tone a 'splendid arrogance'. Alii, 'others', means the Greeks: they will beat out bronze more softly (mollius, with flowing, natural lines), draw living faces from marble, plead causes better, a striking concession in the age of Cicero, and describe the heavens with the rod used for drawing astronomical figures. Conington notes that regere imperio is a Lucretian phrase, that memento is a form of injunction Horace liked, and that Romane in the singular addresses the whole nation, with populos meaning subject peoples. Pacisque imponere morem means to set the custom or rule of peace upon the conquered. Parcere subiectis et debellare superbos became the classic statement of Roman imperial ideology. The poem's last scene tests it, when Aeneas, asked by the defeated Turnus to spare him, sees Pallas' belt and kills him (12.930-52).

title: The young Marcellus (tu Marcellus eris)
greek: heu, miserande puer, si qua fata aspera rumpas, tu Marcellus eris
short: The pageant ends in grief: the young Marcellus, Augustus' nephew and heir, who died in 23 BC aged about nineteen, walks beside his great namesake.
body: Two Marcelli appear. The first is M. Claudius Marcellus, five times consul, who checked Hannibal, defeated the Gauls, and dedicated the spolia opima, the spoils taken by a Roman commander who killed the enemy's commander in single combat, an honour won only three times in Roman history. Beside him walks a beautiful youth with downcast eyes and night around his head. Servius identifies him as Marcellus, son of Augustus' sister Octavia, whom Augustus took as his son; he fell ill and died at Baiae while aedile and was buried with great pomp in the Campus Martius, in the mausoleum Augustus had built (Page: the 'new-made grave' by the Tiber). Servius adds that when Virgil recited the book to Augustus and Octavia, their weeping was so great that they ordered him to stop; the Life by Donatus says that Octavia fainted at 'tu Marcellus eris' and was revived with difficulty. Conington takes the words as 'you shall be a true Marcellus', if you break fate's bonds. The lilies Anchises would scatter are a funeral offering.

title: The gates of Sleep: horn and ivory
greek: sunt geminae Somni portae, quarum altera fertur cornea... altera candenti perfecta nitens elephanto, sed falsa ad caelum mittunt insomnia Manes
short: Aeneas leaves the underworld by the ivory gate, through which false dreams pass: one of the most debated endings in Latin literature.
body: The image comes from Odyssey 19.562-7, where Penelope says that dreams come through two gates, of horn and of ivory; Page explains the Greek puns behind them (keras, horn, with krainein, 'to fulfil'; elephas, ivory, with elephairesthai, 'to deceive'). Virgil makes the horn gate the way for 'true shades' and the ivory gate for false dreams sent up by the dead. Why does Anchises send Aeneas and the Sibyl out by the ivory gate? Servius' plain answer is that the poet 'wants it understood that everything he has said is false', and he adds allegorical explanations (horn as the eyes, ivory as the teeth, i.e. speech). Page proposes a reference to time: dreams before midnight were thought false and those after midnight true (Horace, Satires 1.10.33), so the ivory gate marks the hour of the return. Other suggestions are that Aeneas, being alive, is not a 'true shade' and so cannot use the horn gate, or that the gate casts a deliberate shadow over the glorious pageant. There is no consensus.
